title: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) Methodology
overview: BMR represents the minimum calories your body needs at complete rest to maintain vital functions like breathing, circulation, and cell production. It typically accounts for 60-75% of daily energy expenditure.

methods.name: Mifflin-St Jeor Equation
methods.description: The most accurate predictive equation for BMR according to systematic reviews. Recommended by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics for healthy adults.

formula.name: Mifflin-St Jeor
formula.expression:
Men: BMR = (10 × weight) + (6.25 × height) - (5 × age) + 5
Women: BMR = (10 × weight) + (6.25 × height) - (5 × age) - 161

limitations: Does not account for metabolic adaptations

methods.name: Harris-Benedict (Revised 1984)
methods.description: Updated version of the classic 1918 formula with improved coefficients based on modern data.
limitations: Original 1918 coefficients were for different population

methods.name: Cunningham Equation
methods.description: A lean body mass-based equation that's particularly accurate for athletic populations with higher muscle mass.
methods.accuracy: Best for athletes with known body composition

sources.name: Mifflin et al. - American Journal of Clinical Nutrition

footnotes: BMR differs from RMR (Resting Metabolic Rate) which is slightly higher
BMR decreases approximately 1-2% per decade after age 20
Muscle mass is the primary driver of BMR variation
disclaimer: BMR is an estimate. True BMR can only be measured via indirect calorimetry. Use as a starting point and adjust based on results.
